title: Expected value & fair games
examples: How do I calculate the expected value for a game with multiple steps?
If the expected value is zero, does that always mean the game is fair?
Can you give an example of a game that is not fair?

explain.say: Today we learn about expected value in games. It tells us the average outcome. We calculate this by multiplying outcomes by their probabilities.

items: Expected value is the average outcome.
Calculate by multiplying outcomes by probabilities.

explain.say: Let us say a simple coin toss game. You win three pounds if it is heads. You lose one pound if it is tails. The probability for each is one half.
The expected value is calculated by three pounds times one half, plus negative one pound times one half. This equals one pound.
If the expected value is zero, the game is considered fair. This means you expect to neither win nor lose money over time.

items: Neither win nor lose over time.

faq.q: What does expected value actually mean for a single game?
faq.a: It does not mean you will win exactly that amount on one try. It is the long-term average result over many plays.
asks: Is it the guaranteed win amount?

faq.q: If the expected value is positive, what does that tell me?
faq.a: It suggests that over many plays, you are expected to win money. The game favours the player.
asks: Does a positive E(X) mean I win?
What does a positive expected value imply?

faq.q: How do I know if a game is fair just by looking at the rules?
faq.a: You must calculate the expected value. If that value equals zero, then the game is mathematically fair.
asks: Is there a quick way to check for fairness?
What value proves a game is fair?

faq.q: Does the expected value change if I change the probabilities?
faq.a: Yes, absolutely. The probabilities are key inputs into the calculation. Changing them changes the result.
asks: If probabilities change, does E(X) change?

faq.q: Can I use expected value for things other than money?
faq.a: Yes, you can use it for any numerical outcome. The concept remains the same regardless of what is being measured.
asks: Can I use this for something non-monetary?

facts: Expected value is the sum of each outcome multiplied by its probability.
If the expected value is zero, the game is considered fair.
A positive expected value suggests a potential gain over many trials.
The formula is E(X) equals the sum of x times P(x).

quiz.say: A game has outcomes of one point and zero points. The probabilities are one half and one half respectively. What is the expected value?
quiz.why: The expected value is one point times one half, plus zero points times one half, which equals one half.

wrong.0: This incorrectly multiplies the outcomes by the square of the probability.
wrong.2: This incorrectly adds the outcomes together, ignoring the probabilities.
wrong.3: This incorrectly assumes that the outcomes must cancel each other out.

quiz.say: In a game, you win five pounds with probability one quarter. What is the expected value?
quiz.why: The expected value is five pounds times one quarter, which equals one and one quarter pounds.

wrong.0: This incorrectly multiplies the outcome by the reciprocal of the probability.
wrong.1: This incorrectly calculates the expected value as just the winning amount.
wrong.2: This incorrectly calculates the expected value by dividing the outcome by the probability.

quiz.say: A game pays out one pound if you guess correctly, with a one third probability. If you guess incorrectly, you lose two pounds with a two thirds probability. Is this game fair?

options.show: negative one third of a pound
options.say: negative one third of a pound

quiz.why: The expected value is one pound times one third, plus negative two pounds times two thirds, which equals negative one pound.

wrong.0: This assumes the game is fair when the calculation shows a loss.
wrong.1: This only considers the losing outcome and ignores the winning outcome.
wrong.2: This incorrectly calculates the weighted average by only using the probabilities.
